title: Rate and extent of chemical change flash cards

cards.front: What is activation energy?
back: The minimum energy particles must have for a successful reaction.

cards.front: Which rate unit applies when measuring moles consumed per second?
back: mol s⁻¹.

cards.front: What does a horizontal product–time graph show?
back: No further measured product formation.

cards.front: What does ⇌ represent?
back: A reversible reaction.

cards.front: What must be equal at dynamic equilibrium?
back: Forward and reverse reaction rates.

cards.front: What is meant by a closed reaction system?
back: Reactants and products cannot escape.

cards.front: What solid makes thiosulfate/acid mixtures cloudy?
back: Sulfur.

cards.front: Calculate mean rate when 72 cm³ gas forms in 90 s.
back: Mean rate = 72/90.

cards.front: Calculate molar rate if 0.020 mol reactant is used in 40 s.
Explain why higher concentration usually speeds a solution reaction.
back: More reactant particles occupy each unit volume.
There are **more frequent successful collisions**.

cards.front: Explain why increased gas pressure at the same temperature can increase rate.
back: Reacting gas particles are closer together.
Collisions occur **more frequently**, increasing successful collisions per second.

cards.front: Explain why a powder reacts faster than the same mass of large pieces.
back: Powder has greater **exposed surface area**.
More particles are available for collisions at the solid surface.

cards.front: Explain how a catalyst increases reaction rate.
back: It provides a **different pathway**.
This pathway has **lower activation energy**.

cards.front: Why must a stopper be fitted quickly during gas collection?
back: Gas starts forming as soon as reactants mix.
A delay lets gas escape, underestimating collected volume or altering measured endpoint time.

cards.front: Explain why reaction rate commonly decreases as a batch reaction proceeds.
back: Reactants are used up, reducing their concentration.
Successful collisions become **less frequent**.

cards.front: Explain why equilibrium does not mean equal amounts of reactant and product.
back: Equilibrium requires **equal rates**, not equal quantities.
Constant concentrations can be unequal while both reactions continue.

cards.front: An exothermic forward reaction releases 80 kJ for a stated quantity. What is the reverse energy change?
back: The reverse reaction is **endothermic**.
It absorbs **80 kJ** for the corresponding quantity.

cards.front: For A+B ⇌ C, predict the change after adding A and explain it.
back: Equilibrium shifts **towards C**.
More added A is used, opposing the concentration increase.

cards.front: For A+B ⇌ C, predict the change after removing C.
back: Equilibrium shifts **towards products**.
More C forms, opposing its removal.

cards.front: What is a catalyst’s effect on equilibrium yield and time to equilibrium?
back: **No change in equilibrium yield/position**.
Equilibrium is reached faster because both directions are accelerated.

cards.front: Explain the effect of higher temperature using collision theory.
back: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster.
Collisions occur more frequently.
A greater proportion has energy **at least equal to activation energy**, so more successful collisions occur per second.

cards.front: A tangent has points (20 s, 18 cm³) and (60 s, 46 cm³). Calculate instantaneous rate.
back: Volume change = 46−18 = **28 cm³**.
Time change = 60−20 = **40 s**.

cards.front: The same turbidity endpoint is reached in 80 s and 50 s. Calculate the rate proxies and their ratio.
back: The 50 s condition is **1.6 times as fast** for this endpoint.

cards.front: Explain why reducing temperature can increase equilibrium yield but slow production in an exothermic reaction.
back: Cooling favours the **exothermic direction**, increasing equilibrium product proportion.
Particles move more slowly and collide less frequently.
Fewer collisions exceed activation energy, reducing rate.

cards.front: For N₂(g)+3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), explain the effect of increased pressure on ammonia yield.
back: Reactant side has **four gas moles**, product side two.
Increased pressure favours the side with **fewer gas moles**.
Equilibrium shifts towards ammonia, increasing its yield.

cards.front: For H₂(g)+I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), explain why pressure does not shift equilibrium position.
back: Each side has **two gas moles**.
Neither side reduces the gas-molecule total relative to the other.
Pressure changes can affect reaction rates while leaving equilibrium position unchanged.

cards.front: Describe the reversible changes in hydrated copper sulfate when heated and then treated with water.
back: Heating removes water and changes **blue hydrated** copper sulfate to **white anhydrous** copper sulfate.
Adding water restores the blue hydrated form.
Dehydration absorbs energy; reverse hydration releases energy.

cards.front: Why might two concentrations give different final gas volumes even with the same marble-chip mass?
back: Changing concentration at fixed acid volume changes the amount of acid.
At low concentration, acid may be the **limiting reactant**.
If less carbonate reacts completely, less total gas forms; this is a yield difference as well as a rate difference.

cards.front: Describe how to calculate rate at a chosen point on a curved product–time graph.
back: Draw a tangent touching the curve at the chosen time.
Choose two well-separated points on the tangent, using actual axis scales.
Calculate Δproduct/Δtime from a large triangle.
State correct units; a chord gives an average over an interval instead.

cards.front: Explain a catalyst’s effects on a reaction energy profile and on equilibrium.
back: Alternative pathway has lower **activation-energy peak**.
Reactant/product energy levels and overall energy transfer stay unchanged.
Forward and reverse reactions both become faster.
Equilibrium is reached sooner, with **unchanged equilibrium position**.

cards.front: Explain why the disappearing-cross experiment needs controlled total volume and viewing conditions.
back: Volume and flask shape affect solution depth.
Different depth changes how much cloudiness hides the cross.
Lighting, cross and observer affect endpoint judgement.
Keeping these constant makes time comparisons better reflect concentration-dependent rate.

cards.front: An exothermic equilibrium is 2A(g) ⇌ B(g). Explain the effects of cooling and reducing pressure separately.
back: Cooling favours the **exothermic forward direction**.
This increases B’s equilibrium proportion.
Reducing pressure favours the side with **more gas moles**, two on the left versus one on the right.
This decreases B’s equilibrium proportion; the two changes oppose each other, so no combined amount can be calculated without more data.
